Consistent with the risk_management silo ruling. Two real items for this silo: (1) the implementation is IQAE, not canonical QAE - worth naming for chapter precision; (2) the source frames MC as 'to a lesser extent' suitable than brute-force enumeration - the memo flips this to MC as the primary quantum target, which matters for this silo's themes. #3, #4, #5 are cosmetic or already covered in key_points 3 and 5.

Consistent with the derivative_pricing silo ruling. #2 and #5 are the real ones: the paper is a threshold roadmap, not achieved advantage - 'out of reach of current systems' needs to be explicit; and the hardware gap is 10 kHz current vs 10 MHz required (3 orders of magnitude), not just '10 kHz is too slow.' #4 is worth a light add: re-param wins even when Grover-Rudolph's main weakness is removed. #1 and #3 are cosmetic.

All four flags are cosmetic or cut in the direction the memo already takes. #4 over-fires - the production-scale pessimism is throughout the memo. #3 notes an undemonstrated mitigation hope the source only asserts as future work. Clean load-bearing benchmark cite.

Consistent with the derivative_pricing silo ruling. Three real items: (a) state prep is excluded from the complexity analysis and may be O(2^n) - the paper's headline honesty point; (b) errors stay >10% until ~9 qubits, so the scaling validation does not yet reach usable accuracy in the feasible range; (c) the 100x MC uncertainty gap widens another 10-100x against importance sampling/quasi-MC. Without these the cite reads as a cleaner endorsement than the paper actually offers.

Same pattern as the risk_management silo ruling - all three major flags over-fire on a full memo read. Noise-collapse-to-50% is in key_point 4 verbatim, resource scaling is in key_point 5, shared-factor-loading restriction is in the limitations text. L3 read individual sentences in isolation and missed the cross-coverage.

#2/#3 and #5 are the real ones. The no-PE-AE variant is Suzuki et al.'s - this paper applies it, not originates it. And qGAN is a partial workaround: it has training cost and only outperforms generic loading when warm-started near the target. Both matter for any chapter citing this as the canonical AE-for-options framework. #1 and #4 are cosmetic.

Same pattern as the risk_management ruling - all flags largely over-fire on a full memo read. #3 misreads the memo (it states the experimental on-par result, not the theoretical Manzano bound). #2 is already in the limitations paragraph. #1 is mild emphasis slack - the Npaths-can-kill-speedup is in the memo, just not starkly foregrounded. #4 is subjective.

Consistent with the risk_management silo ruling, all three substantive groups confirmed. Three items: (a) the benchmark - single-asset European option - is analytically solvable without MC; the crossover only materialises at ~10^-10 statistical error; (b) the 4.9x10^5 vs 3.7x10^6 s runtime assumes all-to-all FT-quantum (gate error 10^-3, surface code d=18, 1us cycle) vs single-core 3.1 GHz classical; (c) ELF-style depth reduction gives sub-quadratic speedup - the paper says this explicitly.

Consistent with the risk_management ruling. The QCoin attribution is the real one: the algorithm is from Aaronson & Rall et al. - the NEASQC contribution is applying it to the pricing/risk pipeline, not introducing it. The NISQ-scope and 'huge challenges remain open' framing is worth a light add, but key_point 4 already carries most of the weight. #4, #5, #6 are cosmetic.

All five flags are cosmetic or mild precision slack - the headline 16x/4x reductions and pipeline decomposition are clean. The single-variable limit is adequate for the applications studied (the memo implies a blocker where the paper says 'sufficient here'). The differentiability framing is a minor overgeneralisation. Neither changes any silo theme attribution.

Two real items: (a) both regimes are assumed observable - the paper explicitly excludes latent-state filtering, which is the empirically harder case; (b) the one-hot vs binary comparison holds only for M<=64 on IBM Torino - beyond that neither encoding is currently feasible. #3 and #5 are already covered or false positives. #4 is largely in the memo already.

#1 is the only real one: the ~50x T-depth reduction is amplitude-loading-module-scoped (2.1e3 -> ~40), not a whole-payoff-pipeline reduction - a chapter citing that number needs the scope qualifier. #2 is a false positive, the conditional is verbatim in the memo. #3 is contract-mechanic detail that does not affect silo theme attribution. #4 is cosmetic.

Two real items: (a) independent-assets assumption - real marginals but independent joint; the larger-basket overshoot is attributed by the source to this, not just dimensionality; (b) the 3-4-qubit sweet spot is forced by exponential grid-doubling, not just diminishing accuracy returns. #3 is cosmetic - overshoot dominates the empirical examples even if the source hedges to 'overshoot or undershoot.'

Same as the derivative_pricing ruling - all major flags over-fire on a full memo read. The barrier-option counter-finding (worsening with D_max) is in key_point 5 verbatim. #3 is cosmetic standard-motivation framing. Unusually honest memo, do not touch it.

Approved with caveat on (a) QAE/QML speedup claims belong to primary sources cited in this review, not to Orus et al., and (b) the error-correction-overhead caveat ("speedup vanished under end-to-end EC accounting") needs to be explicit.

Two real items: (a) simulator-only, Qiskit-built lognormal loader - the paper itself says 'true quantum advantage difficult in the short term,' and the 99% accuracy is conditional on appropriate sampling-qubit configuration; MLE's edge holds mainly at small sample sizes (both QAE and MLE converge to O(1/M) eventually); (b) the L-block polynomial loading inherits from Qiskit's built-in uncertainty module, not a novel loading theorem from this paper. Both context points need to ride with the headline 99%/15%/3x numbers.

Two real items: (a) the method targets E_samp, not E_true - the AE quadratic speedup drives Delta_Est to the sampling floor Delta_TrSm, after which total error converges to that floor, not below it; (b) full qubit-reduction requires FT-EC since the deep circuits are not performable on near-term hardware without error correction, and the method requires integrands expressible step-by-step with each random number. Both conditions need to ride with any chapter citation of the speedup and applicability claims.

#4 is the only real one: TCI and the O(N chi^2) black-box scaling are from prior work (Nunez Fernandez 2022, Ritter 2024) - this paper's contribution is the extension for state-prep combined with the V-layer/epsilon_trunc pipeline. A chapter citing the O(N chi^2) scaling as this paper's result would misattribute it. #1 is cosmetic for finance PDFs (real-valued). #3 and #5 are largely covered in dimension_2 and dimension_5 respectively. Unusually thorough memo otherwise.

Two real items: (a) the paper is explicitly positioned as a response to the speedup-may-be-negated critique - QMC's theoretical speedup 'may be substantially reduced or even negated' once state-prep overhead is counted; that motivation is the paper's context and should ride with any citation; (b) the KS = 7.2e-5 headline holds only up to ~15 qubits - beyond that precision degrades even with larger bond dimension, and multivariate quantization requires non-trivial strategy choices (sequential/mirroring/interleaving). #1, #2, #6 are cosmetic.

Two real items: (a) the contribution is positioned as a fourth class of efficient state-prep technique complementary to existing approaches (log-concave, qGAN-learned, quantum-arithmetic) - not a general-purpose replacement; (b) the demo uses MLAE which lacks theoretical guarantees and shows numerical instability at small qubit counts (3-qubit error spike reported in the paper). #1 and the threshold-dominates point are already in the memo.

#1/#2 are the real ones: the O(d*n) 'linear scaling' is at fixed d, and the paper itself says d's independence from n is unproven future work - if d grows with n, the scaling could be O(n^2) or worse. That qualifier needs to ride with any chapter citation of the linear-scaling claim. #3 is mild attribution slack worth noting: the multivariate-credit-risk-QAE framework is from [16], [17]; this paper's contribution is the QSVT state-prep replacement. #4 is cosmetic.
